items.title: Governors-General of Bengal (1773-1833): Hastings to Wellesley
items.body:
**In one line** The first four heads of British India in Bengal — Hastings, Cornwallis, Shore and Wellesley — and the Act or system each is remembered for.

**Why it is asked** Matching a Governor-General to his reform or Act (Regulating Act, Permanent Settlement, Subsidiary Alliance) is a staple one-mark and match-the-following question.

**The story**

Once the Company became a territorial ruler after 1765, London wanted to control it. The **Regulating Act of 1773** created a single head for British India and made **Warren Hastings** the **first Governor-General of Bengal (1772–1785)**. He set up the **Supreme Court at Fort William (1774)** and, with William Jones, founded the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)**; **Pitt's India Act (1784)** also fell in his time. Next, **Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793)** reorganised the administration — he is the **'Father of Civil Services in India'** — introduced the **Permanent Settlement (1793)**, and signed the **Treaty of Seringapatam** ending the Third Anglo-Mysore War. **Sir John Shore (1793–1798)** followed a policy of **non-intervention**. Then **Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)** turned aggressive: his **Subsidiary Alliance** brought Indian states under British protection and control, he signed the **Treaty of Bassein**, and he founded **Fort William College (1800)** to train Company officials.

**Picture it**

| Act | Year | Governor-General |
|---|---|---|
| Regulating Act | 1773 | Warren Hastings |
| Pitt's India Act | 1784 | Warren Hastings |
| Charter Act | 1793 | John Shore |
| Charter Act | 1813 | Lord Minto I |
| Charter Act | 1833 | Lord William Bentinck |
| Charter Act | 1853 | Lord Dalhousie |
| Charter Act | 1853 | Lord Dalhousie |

**Terms explained**

- **Governor-General** — the single head of all the Company's Indian provinces (from 1773).
- **Permanent Settlement** — a land-tax deal (1793) fixing the revenue the zamindar must pay *forever*.
- **Subsidiary Alliance** — Wellesley's system by which an Indian ruler kept (and paid for) a British army and gave up an independent foreign policy.

**Don't confuse** **Cornwallis** = Permanent Settlement and civil-service reform; **Wellesley** = Subsidiary Alliance and Fort William College. Keep the two apart.

**Remember it** Bengal GG order **H-C-S-W**: **H**astings → **C**ornwallis → **S**hore → **W**ellesley.

**TL;DR**

- Warren Hastings = first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773); Asiatic Society (1784).
- Cornwallis = Permanent Settlement (1793); Father of Civil Services.
- Wellesley = Subsidiary Alliance (1798); Fort William College (1800).
- Pitt's India Act (1784) under Hastings; Charter Act 1813 under Minto I, 1833 under Bentinck.
keyPoints: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773) and founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784).
Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement (1793) and is called the Father of Civil Services in India.
Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system and founded Fort William College (1800).
Pitt's India Act (1784) was passed during Warren Hastings' tenure.
The Charter Act of 1813 fell under Lord Minto I and the Charter Act of 1833 under Lord William Bentinck.
Charter Act of 1853 (the last Charter Act) was passed under Lord Dalhousie.
items.mnemonic: Bengal GG order: 'Hastings Cornwallis Shore Wellesley' — H-C-S-W.

items.title: Reforming Governors-General: Bentinck & Dalhousie
items.body:
**In one line** The two great reforming Governors-General — Bentinck, the social reformer, and Dalhousie, the moderniser and annexer.

**Why it is asked** Abolition of Sati, the English Education Act, the first railway, the Doctrine of Lapse and Wood's Dispatch are repeat facts and are easily mixed between the two.

**The story**

**Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835)** was the most liberal Governor-General of the Company era. On the social side he **abolished Sati in 1829** and suppressed **Thuggee** and infanticide. On education he backed the **English Education Act (1835)**, which made English the medium of higher learning — earning him the title **'Father of modern Western education in India'**. The **Charter Act of 1833** made him the **first Governor-General of India** and declared that no Indian should be barred from office because of religion, birth, descent or colour. Two decades later **Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856)** modernised the country's infrastructure: the first **railway line (Bombay–Thane, 1853)**, about 4,000 miles of **telegraph lines connecting the major cities** (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Peshawar), and the **Post Office Act (1854)**. He implemented **Wood's Dispatch (1854)**, the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'. But his **Doctrine of Lapse** — annexing states (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur) whose rulers died without a natural heir — bred deep resentment that helped spark the 1857 revolt.

**Picture it**

| Governor-General | Social / education | Modernisation / expansion |
|---|---|---|
| Bentinck (1828–35) | Abolished Sati (1829); English Education Act (1835) | First GG of India (Charter Act 1833) |
| Dalhousie (1848–56) | Wood's Dispatch (1854) | Railway (1853), telegraph, post; Doctrine of Lapse |

**Terms explained**

- **Sati** — the practice of a widow burning on her husband's funeral pyre; banned in 1829.
- **Doctrine of Lapse** — Dalhousie's rule that a princely state with no *natural* heir would 'lapse' to the Company (adopted heirs not recognised).
- **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** — a plan for a graded education system with universities and grants-in-aid.

**Don't confuse** **Bentinck** = Sati abolition + English education; **Dalhousie** = Doctrine of Lapse + railways/telegraph. The Doctrine of Lapse is **not** Cornwallis's or Bentinck's.

**Remember it** Dalhousie = **Doctrine + Development** (Doctrine of Lapse plus railways, telegraph and post).

**TL;DR**

- Bentinck abolished Sati (1829) and was the first Governor-General of India (Charter Act 1833).
- Bentinck backed the English Education Act (1835).
- Dalhousie opened the first railway (Bombay–Thane, 1853) and introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.
- Dalhousie implemented Wood's Dispatch (1854) and laid the telegraph and postal systems.
keyPoints: Lord William Bentinck abolished Sati in 1829 and became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833.
Bentinck backed the English Education Act (1835) and is called the Father of modern Western education in India.
Lord Dalhousie opened the first railway line (Bombay-Thane) in 1853 and introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.
Dalhousie implemented Wood's Dispatch (1854) and laid the telegraph and postal systems.
Wood's Dispatch (1854) is called the Magna Carta of English education in India.
items.mnemonic: Dalhousie = 'Doctrine + Development' — Doctrine of Lapse plus railways, telegraph, post.

items.title: Lord Canning & the Transition to Crown Rule (1858)
items.body:
**In one line** How Lord Canning bridged the end of Company rule and the start of direct British Crown rule in 1858.

**Why it is asked** 'Last Governor-General / first Viceroy', the Government of India Act 1858 and the Indian Councils Act 1861 are classic transition facts.

**The story**

**Lord Canning (1856–1862)** had the unusual distinction of being the **last Governor-General** of the Company era and then the **first Viceroy of India**. His tenure was dominated by the **Revolt of 1857**, after which the British decided to end Company rule. He had already set up the **universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (1857)**. The **Government of India Act 1858** then **abolished the East India Company** and transferred all power to the **British Crown**; the **Queen's Proclamation** of 1858 promised religious toleration and an end to further annexations. The army was reorganised to raise the ratio of British to Indian troops. A few years later the **Indian Councils Act 1861** introduced the **portfolio system** (each member taking charge of a department) and began the slow return of Indians to law-making.

**Picture it**

| Step | Year | What changed |
|---|---|---|
| Revolt of 1857 | 1857 | Triggered the end of Company rule |
| Presidency universities | 1857 | Calcutta, Madras, Bombay |
| Government of India Act | 1858 | EIC abolished; Crown takes over |
| Queen's Proclamation | 1858 | Toleration; no more annexation |
| Indian Councils Act | 1861 | Portfolio system |

**Terms explained**

- **Viceroy** — the title (meaning the monarch's personal representative) given to the Governor-General after 1858, when he ruled on behalf of the Crown.
- **Portfolio system** — each council member is put in charge of one department (like a modern minister).
- **Paramountcy** — the Crown's supreme authority over the Indian princely states.

**Don't confuse** The **Regulating Act of 1773** created the office of Governor-General of **Bengal**; the **Government of India Act 1858** created direct **Crown rule** and the **Viceroy** title — do not swap the two Acts.

**Remember it** Canning 'closes the Company' — the GoI Act 1858 ends EIC rule.

**TL;DR**

- Lord Canning was the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India.
- The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the EIC and gave power to the Crown.
- Canning set up the Calcutta, Madras and Bombay universities (1857).
- The Indian Councils Act 1861 brought in the portfolio system.
keyPoints: Lord Canning was the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India.
The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the British Crown.
Canning established the universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1857.
The Indian Councils Act 1861 introduced the portfolio (budget) system.
The Revolt of 1857 unfolded during Canning's tenure and triggered Crown rule.
items.mnemonic: Canning 'closes the Company' — GoI Act 1858 ends EIC rule.

items.title: Early Viceroys: Mayo, Lytton, Ripon & Dufferin
items.body:
**In one line** The first generation of Viceroys (1869–1888) — Mayo, Lytton, Ripon and Dufferin — and the measures that both built the administration and stirred nationalism.

**Why it is asked** The 'press seesaw' (Lytton imposes, Ripon repeals), the first Census, the Ilbert Bill and the founding of the Congress are high-frequency facts.

**The story**

After Crown rule settled in, **Lord Mayo (1869–1872)** introduced **financial decentralisation** (giving provinces control of some budgets) and held the first regular **Census (1872)**; he founded Mayo College and was **assassinated at Port Blair**. **Lord Lytton (1876–1880)** turned repressive: the **Vernacular Press Act** gagged Indian-language newspapers, the **Arms Act** disarmed Indians, and he held a grand **Durbar (1877)** proclaiming **Queen Victoria 'Empress of India'** — all during a severe famine, which deepened anger. His successor **Lord Ripon (1880–1884)** reversed course: he **repealed the Vernacular Press Act**, extended **local self-government** (so he is the **'Father of Local Self-Government'**), and proposed the **Ilbert Bill** to let Indian judges try Europeans. The furious European backlash to the Bill ironically showed Indians the power of organised protest, and in **1885**, under **Lord Dufferin (1884–1888)**, the **Indian National Congress** was founded.

**Picture it**

| Viceroy | Tenure | Remembered for |
|---|---|---|
| Mayo | 1869–1872 | Financial decentralisation; first Census (1872) |
| Lytton | 1876–1880 | Vernacular Press Act; Arms Act; Victoria 'Empress' (1877) |
| Ripon | 1880–1884 | Repealed Press Act; local self-government; Ilbert Bill |
| Dufferin | 1884–1888 | Founding of the INC (1885) |

**Terms explained**

- **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** — a law to control newspapers printed in Indian languages.
- **Local self-government** — elected municipal and district boards running local affairs; Ripon's reform of 1882.
- **Ilbert Bill** — a proposal to let Indian magistrates try European defendants, which Europeans fiercely opposed.

**Don't confuse** **Lytton imposed** the Vernacular Press Act (1878); **Ripon repealed** it (1882). Do not reverse the two.

**Remember it** Press seesaw: **Lytton locks** the press, **Ripon releases** it.

**TL;DR**

- Mayo: financial decentralisation and the first Census (1872); assassinated at Port Blair.
- Lytton: Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act, Victoria proclaimed Empress (1877).
- Ripon: repealed the Press Act; Father of Local Self-Government; Ilbert Bill.
- INC founded in 1885 under Dufferin.
keyPoints: Lord Mayo introduced financial decentralisation and conducted the first Census (1872); he was assassinated at Port Blair.
Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act and proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India (1877).
Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act and is the Father of Local Self-Government; he introduced the Ilbert Bill.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 during Lord Dufferin's viceroyalty.
Lytton imposed the Vernacular Press Act (1878); Ripon repealed it (1882).
items.mnemonic: Press seesaw: Lytton locks the press, Ripon releases it.

items.title: Curzon, Minto II & Hardinge II: Partition Politics
items.body:
**In one line** The Viceroys of the partition years — Curzon who split Bengal, Minto II who brought separate electorates, and Hardinge II who undid the partition.

**Why it is asked** Partition of Bengal (1905), the Morley–Minto Reforms (1909), the Muslim League (1906) and the capital shift to Delhi (1911) are very frequently asked and easily confused.

**The story**

**Lord Curzon (1899–1905)** was an energetic but high-handed Viceroy. He passed the **Indian Universities Act** and, most fatefully, **partitioned Bengal in 1905** — officially for administrative ease, but widely seen as dividing Hindus and Muslims. The partition sparked the **Swadeshi Movement**. (Curzon also strengthened the **Archaeological Survey of India** and conservation.) Under **Lord Minto II (1905–1910)** came the **Morley–Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909)**, which introduced **separate electorates** — seats reserved for Muslims, voted on only by Muslims — formalising communal politics; the **Muslim League** had been founded in **1906**. Finally **Lord Hardinge II (1910–1916)** calmed opinion by **annulling the Partition of Bengal** and **shifting the capital from Calcutta to Delhi**, both announced at the **1911 Delhi Durbar**. The Hindu Mahasabha was formed during his tenure.

**Picture it**

| Viceroy | Tenure | Partition-era landmark |
|---|---|---|
| Curzon | 1899–1905 | Partition of Bengal (1905); Universities Act |
| Minto II | 1905–1910 | Morley–Minto Reforms / separate electorates (1909) |
| Hardinge II | 1910–1916 | Annulled partition; capital to Delhi (1911) |

**Terms explained**

- **Partition of Bengal** — Curzon's 1905 split of the Bengal province into two.
- **Separate electorates** — a system where a community (here Muslims) votes only for its own reserved seats.
- **Swadeshi Movement** — the boycott of British goods and promotion of Indian-made goods that began against the partition.

**Don't confuse** **Curzon partitioned** Bengal (1905); **Hardinge II annulled** it (1911). The Morley–Minto Reforms belong to **Minto II**, not Morley alone.

**Remember it** **Curzon cuts** Bengal (1905); **Hardinge heals** it (1911) and moves the capital to Delhi.

**TL;DR**

- Curzon partitioned Bengal (1905) and brought the Indian Universities Act.
- Morley–Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates — under Minto II.
- Muslim League founded 1906 (Minto II's time).
- Hardinge II annulled the partition and shifted the capital to Delhi (announced 1911).
keyPoints: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 and introduced the Indian Universities Act.
The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introducing separate electorates came under Lord Minto II.
The Muslim League was founded in 1906 during Minto II's tenure.
Lord Hardinge II annulled the Bengal partition and shifted the capital to Delhi (announced 1911).
Curzon's tenure strengthened the Archaeological Survey of India.
items.mnemonic: Curzon cuts Bengal (1905); Hardinge heals it (1911) and moves to Delhi.

items.title: Late Viceroys: Chelmsford to Mountbatten
items.body:
**In one line** The last Viceroys (1916–1948), from Chelmsford to Mountbatten, whose policies and crises carried India to independence.

**Why it is asked** Each is tied to a landmark the exam loves — Montagu–Chelmsford/Jallianwala, Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Quit India, and the June 3rd Plan.

**The story**

**Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921)** gave India the **Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms (1919)**, which introduced **dyarchy** in the provinces, but also the repressive **Rowlatt Act** and the horror of the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919)**. **Lord Reading (1921–1926)** saw the Chauri Chaura incident and the Swaraj Party. **Lord Irwin (1926–1931)** faced the **Civil Disobedience Movement** and the **Dandi (Salt) March (1930)**, hosted the **First Round Table Conference**, and signed the **Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931)**. **Lord Willingdon (1931–1936)** held the Second and Third Round Table Conferences and oversaw the **Communal Award** and the resulting **Poona Pact (1932)**. **Lord Linlithgow (1936–1944)** handled the **Cripps Mission** and the **Quit India Movement (1942)**. **Lord Wavell (1944–1947)** proposed the **CR Formula**, called the **Shimla Conference**, and faced **Direct Action Day (1946)**. Finally **Lord Mountbatten (1947–1948)** announced the **June 3rd Plan** for partition and became the **last Viceroy** and the **first Governor-General of independent India**.

**Picture it**

| Viceroy | Tenure | Landmark |
|---|---|---|
| Chelmsford | 1916–1921 | Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms; Jallianwala Bagh (1919) |
| Irwin | 1926–1931 | Civil Disobedience; Dandi March; Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931) |
| Linlithgow | 1936–1944 | Cripps Mission; Quit India (1942) |
| Wavell | 1944–1947 | CR Formula; Shimla Conference; Direct Action Day (1946) |
| Mountbatten | 1947–1948 | June 3rd Plan; last Viceroy / first GG of free India |

**Terms explained**

- **Dyarchy** — 'double rule': provincial subjects split between elected Indian ministers and British officials.
- **Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931)** — an agreement suspending Civil Disobedience in return for Congress joining the Second Round Table Conference.
- **June 3rd Plan (1947)** — Mountbatten's scheme that led to partition and the Indian Independence Act 1947.

**Don't confuse** The **Dandi March (1930)** was under **Irwin**, not Chelmsford; **Direct Action Day (1946)** was under **Wavell**, before Mountbatten arrived.

**Remember it** Last stretch to freedom: **Chelmsford → Reading → Irwin → Willingdon → Linlithgow → Wavell → Mountbatten.**

**TL;DR**

- Chelmsford: Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms (1919), Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh.
- Irwin: Civil Disobedience, Dandi March (1930), Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931).
- Linlithgow: Cripps Mission and Quit India (1942).
- Wavell: CR Formula, Shimla Conference, Direct Action Day (1946).
- Mountbatten: June 3rd Plan; last Viceroy and first Governor-General of free India.
keyPoints: Lord Chelmsford's tenure saw the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919), the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh.
Lord Irwin saw the Civil Disobedience Movement, the Dandi March (1930) and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931).
Lord Linlithgow managed the Cripps Mission and the Quit India Movement (1942).
Lord Wavell introduced the CR Formula, organised the Shimla Conference and saw Direct Action Day (1946).
Lord Mountbatten proposed the June 3rd Plan and was the last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India.
items.mnemonic: Last five Viceroys: 'Chelmsford Reading Irwin Willingdon Linlithgow ... Wavell Mountbatten'.

items.title: Land Settlements, Educational Institutions & Committees (PYQ set)
items.body:
**In one line** A PYQ cluster — the three land-revenue settlements, the real purpose of the Subsidiary Alliance, early colleges and their founders, and key committees.

**Why it is asked** These exact items have appeared in UPSC prelims (land settlements 2017, Subsidiary Alliance 2018, Butler Committee 2017), so they are high-probability questions.

**The story**

The British tried three ways to collect land tax. The **Permanent (Zamindari) Settlement (1793)** of **Cornwallis** made the **zamindar** the owner and fixed his tax forever; the **Ryotwari Settlement** of **Alexander Read and Thomas Munro** collected directly from the **ryot** (cultivator); the **Mahalwari Settlement** of **Holt Mackenzie and R. M. Bird** collected from the whole village (**mahal**). On the political side, **Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798)** forced an ally to keep and pay for a British force (often by *ceding land* instead of cash), accept a British Resident, and give up independent alliances or wars — it did **not** aim to give the Company a fixed income (a common trap). Education grew through early colleges: the **Calcutta Madarsa (1781)** of Warren Hastings, the **Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791)** of Jonathan Duncan, and **Fort William College (1800)** of Wellesley to train British officials. Later, committees shaped policy — the **Butler Committee (1927)** on Crown–princely-state relations, and earlier the **Hunter Commission (1882)** and **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** on education.

**Picture it**

| Settlement | Author(s) | Region | Revenue paid by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permanent / Zamindari (1793) | Cornwallis (with John Shore) | Bengal, Bihar, Orissa | Zamindar (fixed forever) |
| Ryotwari | Alexander Read & Thomas Munro | Madras & Bombay | Ryot (cultivator) |
| Mahalwari | Holt Mackenzie & R. M. Bird | North-West Provinces, Punjab | Village (mahal) |

**Terms explained**

- **Zamindar** — a landholder made the legal owner and tax-collector under the Permanent Settlement.
- **Ryot** — a peasant cultivator who paid tax directly to the state under the Ryotwari system.
- **Paramountcy** — the supreme authority of the British Crown over the princely states, examined by the Butler Committee.

**Don't confuse** The Subsidiary Alliance was about **troops, a Resident and control of foreign policy — not a fixed income**. And keep the land systems apart: **Ryot**wari = cultivator, **Mahal**wari = village, **Zamindari** = landlord.

**Remember it** Land settlements **RPM**: **R**yotwari (Read/Munro), **P**ermanent (Cornwallis), **M**ahalwari (Mackenzie/Bird).

**TL;DR**

- Permanent (1793, Cornwallis) = Bengal; Ryotwari (Read & Munro) = Madras/Bombay; Mahalwari (Mackenzie & Bird) = NW Provinces.
- Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley 1798) did NOT aim at a fixed income — troops, Resident, no independent alliances.
- Colleges: Calcutta Madarsa (1781) = Hastings; Sanskrit College Benaras (1791) = Duncan; Fort William College (1800) = Wellesley.
- Butler Committee (1927) examined Crown–princely-state (paramountcy) relations.
keyPoints: Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis) — Bengal; Ryotwari (Read & Munro) — Madras/Bombay; Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie & R.M. Bird) — NW Provinces.
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley 1798) did NOT aim to secure a fixed income for the Company — it was about troops, a Resident and no independent alliances.
Fort William College (1800, Wellesley) trained British civil servants for administration.
Calcutta Madarsa (1781) = Warren Hastings; Sanskrit College Benaras (1791) = Jonathan Duncan.
Butler Committee (1927) examined Government of India–princely states (paramountcy) relations.
items.mnemonic: Land settlements RPM: Ryotwari (Read/Munro), Permanent (Cornwallis), Mahalwari (Mackenzie/Bird).

items.title: Governors-General of Bengal 1772–1828 — tenure and every signature measure
items.body:
### Governors-General of Bengal 1772–1828 — tenure and every signature measure

**In one line**
One table: each Governor-General of Bengal, his years and every measure or event an exam pins on him.

**The story**
**Warren Hastings** (**1772**–**1785**) set up the **Supreme Court** (**Impey**), fought the **Rohilla** War, hanged **Nand Kumar**, founded the **Calcutta Madrasa** (**1781**), backed **William Jones** (**1784**) and **Wilkins**'s **Gita**, moved the treasury from **Murshidabad** and set up district **Adalat**s, and was impeached by **Burke** over **Chait Singh**. After **Macpherson**, **Cornwallis** (**1786**–**1793**) issued the **Cornwallis Code** and put the **daroga** over police. **Shore** chose **non-intervention** (**Kharda**) and passed the **Charter Act of 1793**. Wellesley, the **Bengal Tiger**, signed up the **Nizam**, imposed the **Censorship of Press Act**, and organised the **Madras Presidency** (**1801**). **Vellore** rose in **1806** under Barlow; **Minto I** made the **Treaty of Amritsar** (**1809**). Lord Hastings (**Moira**, **1813**) chose **intervention and war**: **Sagauli** (**1816**), the end of the **Peshwaship**, and **Munro** (**1820**). **Adam** imposed the **Licensing Regulation**. Amherst won **Yandabo** (**1826**) and **Assam**, faced **Barrackpore** (**1824**), took **Bharatpur** and opened the **Sanskrit College at Calcutta**.

#### Governor-General → measure

| Governor-General | Measure / event |
|---|---|
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Governor 1772; GG of Bengal 1773–1785 |
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Supreme Court at Calcutta, 1774 (Elijah Impey) |

| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Calcutta Madrasa (1781) |
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Asiatic Society of Bengal — William Jones (1784) |
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Charles Wilkins’s English Gita (1785) |
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Impeachment by Burke over Chait Singh |
| **Warren Hastings (1772–85)** | Treasury Murshidabad → Calcutta; district Adalats (1772) |
| **John Macpherson (1785–86, acting)** | Acting GG after Hastings |
| **Lord Cornwallis (1786–93)** | GG 1786–1793 |
| **Lord Cornwallis (1786–93)** | Cornwallis Code — revenue and justice separated (1793) |
| **Lord Cornwallis (1786–93)** | Thanas under a daroga (police reform) |
| **Sir John Shore (1793–98)** | Non-intervention; Battle of Kharda (1795) |
| **Sir John Shore (1793–98)** | Charter Act of 1793 |
| **Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)** | “Bengal Tiger”; Nizam first subsidiary ally (1798) |
| **Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)** | Censorship of Press Act (1799) |
| **Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)** | Madras Presidency formed (1801) |
| **Sir George Barlow (1805–07)** | Vellore Mutiny (1806) |
| **Lord Minto I (1807–13)** | Treaty of Amritsar with Ranjit Singh (1809) |
| **Lord Hastings (1813–23)** | Lord Moira — GG 1813–1823 |
| **Lord Hastings (1813–23)** | Policy of intervention and war (paramountcy) |
| **Lord Hastings (1813–23)** | Anglo-Nepal War; Treaty of Sagauli (1816) |
| **Lord Hastings (1813–23)** | Pindaris crushed; Peshwaship abolished (1818) |
| **Lord Hastings (1813–23)** | Munro’s ryotwari in Madras (1820) |
| **John Adam (1823, acting)** | Licensing Regulation of 1823 |
| **Lord Amherst (1823–28)** | First Burmese War; Treaty of Yandabo (1826) |
| **Lord Amherst (1823–28)** | Assam annexed |
| **Lord Amherst (1823–28)** | Barrackpore mutiny (1824) |
| **Lord Amherst (1823–28)** | Capture of Bharatpur (1826) |
| **Lord Amherst (1823–28)** | Sanskrit College at Calcutta (1824) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Warren Hastings** (1772–85) ≠ **Lord Hastings / Moira** (1813–23).
- **Minto I** = Treaty of Amritsar 1809; **Minto II** = Morley–Minto 1909.
- **Calcutta Madrasa** = Hastings; **Sanskrit College Benaras** = Jonathan Duncan; **Sanskrit College Calcutta** = 1824 (Amherst).

**TL;DR**
- Hastings: Supreme Court 1774, Madrasa 1781, Asiatic Society 1784, Gita 1785, impeachment.
- Cornwallis Code 1793; Shore — Kharda; Wellesley — Censorship 1799; Barlow — Vellore 1806.
- Minto I — Amritsar 1809; Lord Hastings — Sagauli 1816, Peshwaship ended 1818; Amherst — Yandabo 1826, Assam.
keyPoints: Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Calcutta Madrasa (1781), Asiatic Society (1784) — all under Warren Hastings.
Edmund Burke led the impeachment of Hastings (Chait Singh, Begums of Awadh).
Cornwallis Code (1793) separated revenue and judicial functions.
Shore: non-intervention, Kharda (1795); Barlow: Vellore Mutiny (1806); Minto I: Treaty of Amritsar (1809).
Lord Hastings: Treaty of Sagauli (1816), Peshwaship abolished; Amherst: Treaty of Yandabo (1826), Assam.

items.title: Governors-General 1828–1862 — Bentinck to Canning, measure by measure
items.body:
### Governors-General 1828–1862 — Bentinck to Canning, measure by measure

**In one line**
From the first Governor-General of India to the first Viceroy: every tenure and signature act in one table.

**The story**
**Bentinck** (**1828**–**1835**) passed **Regulation XVII**, used **Sleeman** against the **thug**s, took **Coorg** (**1834**), and acted on **Macaulay**'s **Minute**; the **Calcutta Medical College** opened. Metcalfe, the **Liberator** of the **Press**, opened the **Calcutta Public Library**. Auckland began the **First Anglo-Afghan War** after the **Tripartite Treaty** against **Dost Muhammad**. Ellenborough took **Sindh** (**Napier**) and abolished **slavery** (**Act V**). Hardinge I fought the **First Anglo-Sikh War**. Dalhousie (**1848**–**1856**) used lapse from **Satara** to **Nagpur**, took **Awadh** for **misgovernment**, plus **Pegu**, **Berar** and **Punjab** (**1849**). He opened the **Thane** line on **16 April 1853**, laid **4,000 miles** of **telegraph**, passed the **Post Office Act** (**1854**), and built the **Ganges Canal** and **Public Works**. Canning (**1856**–**1862**) saw the **Widows' Remarriage Act**, the **General Service Enlistment Act**, the **Indian Penal Code** (**1860**), **income tax** (**James Wilson**), the **White Mutiny** and the **High Courts Act**.

**Don't confuse**
- **Awadh (1856)** was annexed for **misgovernment**, not by the Doctrine of Lapse.
- **Licensing Regulation 1823** = Adam; repealed by **Metcalfe** (1835).
- **Widows' Remarriage Act (July 1856)** came under **Canning**, though often credited to Dalhousie's time.

**TL;DR**
- Bentinck: Regulation XVII 1829, Sleeman, Coorg 1834, Macaulay 1835.
- Metcalfe press; Auckland Afghan war; Ellenborough Sindh + slavery 1843; Hardinge I Sikh war.

- Canning: Widow Remarriage 1856, GSEA 1856, IPC 1860, income tax 1860.
keyPoints: Sati was banned by Regulation XVII (1829); William Sleeman suppressed the thugs.
Metcalfe — Liberator of the Indian Press; Auckland — First Anglo-Afghan War and Tripartite Treaty (1838).
Ellenborough annexed Sindh (1843) and abolished slavery (Act V of 1843).
Dalhousie annexed Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur by lapse and Awadh for misgovernment; first railway 16 April 1853.
Under Canning: Widows’ Remarriage Act 1856, General Service Enlistment Act 1856, IPC 1860, first income tax (James Wilson).

items.title: Viceroys 1862–1905 — Elgin I to Curzon, measure by measure
items.body:
### Viceroys 1862–1905 — Elgin I to Curzon, measure by measure

**In one line**
Every Viceroy from Elgin I to Curzon with the acts, wars, commissions and incidents of his tenure.

**The story**
**Elgin I** met the **Wahabi** challenge and died at **Dharamsala**. John Lawrence opened the **High Courts** (**1865**), fought **Bhutan**, kept **masterly inactivity** and created the **Forest Department** (**1864**). Mayo began **financial decentralisation** (**1870**), gave his name to **Mayo College**, **Ajmer**, and set up a **Department of Agriculture**; he was killed by **Sher Ali** at **Port Blair**. Northbrook faced the **Kuka**s, the **Prince of Wales** (**1875**) visit and **Malhar Rao**. Lytton passed the **Royal Titles Act** (**Kaisar-i-Hind**) and the **gagging act**, appointed **Strachey**, began the **Second Anglo-Afghan War**, cut the age to **19** and created the **Statutory Civil Service**. Ripon issued the **Resolution of 1882**, the **Factory Act** (**1881**) and the **census** (**1881**), the **Hunter Commission** (**1882**), and **repealed** the **Vernacular Press Act**. Dufferin took **Upper Burma** and passed the **Bengal Tenancy Act**. Lansdowne: the **Indian Councils Act 1892**, the **Durand Line** (**1893**), the **Age of Consent Act**. Elgin II: **Chapekar** brothers shot **Rand**; **Lyall**. Curzon: **Raleigh** (**1904**), the **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act**, the **North-West Frontier Province**, **Younghusband** in **Tibet**, **Andrew Fraser**, **Kitchener**, the **Calcutta Corporation Act**, **Pusa** and partition on **16 October 1905**.

**Don't confuse**

**TL;DR**
- Elgin I Wahabi; Lawrence High Courts 1865, masterly inactivity; Mayo finance 1870, killed 1872.

items.body:
### Viceroys 1905–1950 — Minto II to Rajagopalachari, measure by measure

**In one line**
Every Viceroy of the freedom-struggle years with the movements, acts and missions of his tenure.

**The story**
Minto II saw the League at **Dacca** (**1906**), the **Surat Split** and the **Newspapers** Act (**1908**). Hardinge II hosted **George V** (**1911**), survived the **Delhi Conspiracy** bomb, and saw **Ghadar**, **Komagata Maru** and the **Hindu Mahasabha** (**1915**). Chelmsford: the **Lucknow Pact**, **Home Rule**, **Champaran** (**1917**), **Saddler**, and **Non-Cooperation** (**1920**). Reading: **Moplah** (**1921**), **Chauri Chaura**, the **Swaraj Party**; he **repealed the Rowlatt Act**; **Kakori**, the **RSS** and the **Communist Party**. Irwin: the **Simon Commission** (**1927**), the **Deepavali Declaration**, the **Sharda Act**, the pact of **5 March 1931**. Willingdon: the **Communal Award**, the **Poona Pact**, the **Government of India Act 1935**, the **Congress Socialist Party**. Linlithgow, the **longest** in office: elections (**1937**), the **August Offer**, the **Pakistan** Resolution, **8 August 1942**. Wavell: the **Wavell Plan** (**1945**), the **RIN Mutiny**, the **Cabinet Mission**, **16 August 1946**, **2 September 1946**. Mountbatten: the **Indian Independence Act**, **Radcliffe**, till **June 1948**; then **Rajagopalachari**, the **first and last Indian** Governor-General.

**TL;DR**
- Minto II: League 1906, Surat 1907; Hardinge II: Durbar 1911, bomb 1912, Ghadar.

items.title: Acts, land settlements and institutions — the linkage table
items.body:
### Acts, land settlements and institutions — the linkage table

**In one line**
The constitutional Acts of Company rule, the three land settlements, and the colleges and commissions — each with its man and year.

**The story**
The Regulating Act gave a **council of four**; the **Act of Settlement** (**1781**) trimmed the court; Pitt's Act created the **Board of Control** and **dual** control; the Act of **1786** let the GG **overrule**. The 1793 Act gave **20 years**; 1813 gave **1 lakh** and admitted **missionaries**; 1833 added a **law member** and **Law Commission**; 1853 brought **open competition** and a **legislative** council; 1858 created the **Secretary of State** with **15** councillors. The Permanent Settlement of **22 March 1793** took **10/11**, enforced by the **Sunset Law**; **John Shore** helped. **Alexander Read** began ryotwari at **Baramahal**; **Elphinstone** and **Wingate** took it to Bombay; it ran in **Coorg** and **Berar**. Mahalwari came with **Regulation VII** (**1822**) and **Regulation IX** (Bird, **Thomason**), with the **headman** paying. **Jonathan Duncan** (**1791**), Fort William (**Indian languages**), **Hindu College** (**David Hare**), Wood (**London**, **grants-in-aid**), Hunter (**primary**), **Hartog**, Butler (**paramountcy**), **MacDonnell** and the **Lee Commission** complete the list. Frontier wars: Afghan I (**1842**, **Dost Muhammad**), **Gandamak**, **Rawalpindi** (**1919**); Nepal ceded **Kumaon** and **Garhwal**; Burma lost **Thibaw**.

#### Acts of Company rule

| Act | Provision |
|---|---|
| **Regulating Act 1773** | GG of Bengal + **council of four**; Bombay and Madras made subordinate; Supreme Court |
| **Act of Settlement 1781** | Divided powers between the GG-in-Council and the Supreme Court |
| **Pitt's India Act 1784** | **Board of Control** in London + Court of Directors = **dual** control |
| **Act of 1786** | GG could **overrule** his council; also Commander-in-Chief (for Cornwallis) |
| **Charter Act 1793** | Monopoly renewed for **20 years** (Shore) |
| **Charter Act 1813** | Rs **1 lakh** for education; **missionaries** allowed; monopoly ended except tea and China |
| **Charter Act 1833** | GG of India; **law member** (Macaulay); first **Law Commission**; Company purely administrative |
| **Charter Act 1853** | **Open competition** for the ICS; separate **legislative** council (6 members); last Charter Act (Dalhousie) |
| **GoI Act 1858** | **Secretary of State** + **15**-member Council of India; GG became Viceroy |

#### Land settlements

| System | Fact |
|---|---|
| Permanent | **22 March 1793**; Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Benares, northern Madras (Circars) |
| Permanent | State share **10/11**, zamindar 1/11 — fixed forever |
| Permanent | **Sunset Law** — estates auctioned for default |
| Permanent | Planned with **John Shore**; ~19% of British India |
| Ryotwari | **Alexander Read** in **Baramahal** (1792); Munro in Madras 1820 |
| Ryotwari | Bombay — **Elphinstone**, **Wingate**; ~51% of British India |
| Ryotwari | Madras, Bombay, Assam, **Coorg**, **Berar**, East Punjab |
| Mahalwari | **Regulation VII** of **1822** — Holt Mackenzie; NWP, Punjab, central India; ~30% |
| Mahalwari | **Regulation IX** of 1833 — R.M. Bird and James **Thomason** |
| Mahalwari | Village **headman** paid for the whole mahal; revenue revised periodically |

#### Institutions and commissions

| Year | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1791** | Sanskrit College, Benares — **Jonathan Duncan** |
| **1800** | Fort William College — Wellesley; trained British civilians in **Indian languages** |
| **1817** | **Hindu College**, Calcutta — **David Hare** and Indian patrons |
| **1854** | Wood's Dispatch — universities on the **London** model, **grants-in-aid**, vernacular primary schools |
| **1882** | Hunter Commission — **primary** and secondary education; local boards to run schools |
| **1929** | **Hartog** Committee — education, under the Simon Commission |
| **1927** | Butler Committee — **paramountcy** must remain supreme |
| **1901** | **MacDonnell** Famine Commission (Curzon) |
| **1923–24** | **Lee Commission** — civil services; Public Service Commission set up 1926 |

#### Frontier wars

| War | GG / Viceroy | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **1st Afghan** (1839–42) | Auckland | Retreat from Kabul massacred; **Dost Muhammad** restored (**1842**) |
| **2nd Afghan** (1878–80) | Lytton | Treaty of **Gandamak** (1879) |
| **3rd Afghan** (**1919**) | Chelmsford | Treaty of **Rawalpindi** — Afghan independence in foreign affairs |
| **Anglo-Nepal** (1814–16) | Lord Hastings | Sagauli — **Kumaon**, **Garhwal** ceded; Resident at Kathmandu |
| **3rd Burmese** (1885) | Dufferin | King **Thibaw** deposed; Upper Burma annexed 1886 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Pitt's India Act 1784** = Board of Control; **Regulating Act 1773** = Supreme Court + council of four.
- **Read** began ryotwari (Baramahal 1792); **Munro** spread it (Madras 1820).
- **Hunter Commission 1882** = education; **Raleigh 1902** = universities; **Hartog 1929**.

**TL;DR**
- 1773 council of four; 1781 Settlement; 1784 Board of Control; 1786 overrule; 1793/1813/1833/1853/1858 Acts.
- Permanent 22 Mar 1793, 10/11, Sunset Law; Ryotwari Read/Munro/Elphinstone; Mahalwari Reg. VII 1822, Reg. IX 1833.
- Duncan 1791, FWC 1800, Hindu College 1817, Wood 1854, Hunter 1882, Butler 1927; Gandamak 1879, Rawalpindi 1919.
keyPoints: Pitt's India Act 1784 set up the Board of Control (dual control); Charter Act 1833 added a law member and the Law Commission.
Charter Act 1853 introduced open competition; GoI Act 1858 created the Secretary of State with a 15-member Council.
Permanent Settlement: state 10/11, Sunset Law; Alexander Read began ryotwari in Baramahal; Mahalwari — Regulation VII of 1822.
Sanskrit College Benares — Jonathan Duncan (1791); Hindu College (1817) — David Hare; Wood’s Dispatch — grants-in-aid.
Treaty of Gandamak (1879) — Second Afghan War; Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919) — Third Afghan War.

items.title: For Mains — Governor-Generals & Viceroys
items.body:
**In one line** For Mains, the Governors-General and Viceroys are asked as a *theme* — how colonial policy modernised India while simultaneously provoking nationalism — not as a name-and-date list.

**Mains dimensions**

**Data points and authorities to quote**

- **Permanent Settlement, 1793** (Cornwallis) — fixed revenue; absentee landlordism and rural stagnation.
- **English Education Act, 1835** and Macaulay's Minute — creating a class 'Indian in blood, English in taste'.
- **Partition of Bengal, 1905** — Curzon's spark for the Swadeshi Movement.
- **Morley–Minto Reforms, 1909** — separate electorates; the institutional seed of communal politics.
- **Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms, 1919** — dyarchy, the first step towards responsible government.

**AP angle** The Ryotwari settlement shaped agrarian relations across the Telugu districts of the Madras Presidency, while mission schools and English education produced the reformers (e.g. Kandukuri Veeresalingam) and the educated middle class that led the Andhra reform and nationalist movements, and the Swadeshi/Vandemataram agitation spread strongly in coastal Andhra.

**Use in answers**

- *Example to cite:* the Ilbert Bill backlash (1883) as the moment Indians learnt the value of organised agitation.
- *Quote:* Macaulay's Minute (1835) when discussing colonial education policy.
- *Diagram idea:* a timeline bar — 'Reform ↔ Repression' — placing each Viceroy's liberal and coercive measures side by side.
